question: How tall is the Burj Khalifa in meters?
raw_answer: The Burj Khalifa is 828 meters tall in architectural height [4]. Its total height to the tip, including the spire, is 829.8 meters [4].

passages.heading: Ranking criteria and alternatives
passages.text: Until 1996, the world's tallest building was defined by the height to the top of the tallest architectural element, including spires but not antennae.<sup>[8]</sup> In 1930, this definitional argument led to a rivalry between the Bank of Manhattan Building and the Chrysler Building. The Bank of Manhattan Building (i.e. 40 Wall Street) employed only a short spire, was 282.5 m (927 ft) tall, and had a much higher top occupied floor (the second category in the 1996 criteria for tallest building). In contrast, the Chrysler Building employed a very large 38 m (125 ft) spire secretly assembled inside the building to claim the title of world's tallest building with a total height of 319 m (1046 ft), although it had a lower top occupied floor and a shorter height when both buildings' spires were excluded.<sup>[*citation needed*]</sup>

passages.heading: Alternative measurements / Height to pinnacle (highest point)
passages.text:
This measurement only recently came into use, when the Petronas Towers passed the Sears Tower (now named Willis Tower) in height. The former was considered taller because its spires were considered architectural, while the latter's antennae were not. This led to the split of definitions, with the Sears Tower claiming the lead in this and the height-to-roof (now highest occupied floor) categories, and with the Petronas claiming the lead in the architectural height category.

If the original World Trade Center towers were still standing, the North (1,728 feet (526.7 m), including the antenna) and South Towers (1,377 feet (419.7 m)) would fall between numbers 11 and 37 on the current list (as it can be assumed the rebuilt One World Trade Center would have never been built).

passages.text: In the history of architecture, height has never been a neutral ambition. From Gothic cathedrals reaching toward the heavens to early skyscrapers signaling industrial confidence, verticality has consistently carried cultural meaning alongside technical challenge. Standing at 828 meters (2,717 feet) with 163 floors, the Burj Khalifa in the United Arab Emirates emerges from this lineage not simply as a record-breaking object, but as a contemporary expression of how architecture, engineering, capital, and global identity converge. Rising from the desert landscape of Dubai, the tower is at once a feat of structural ingenuity and a symbol of a city repositioning itself within a global network of finance, tourism, and spectacle. To understand how many floors the Burj Khalifa has—and why each matters—is to engage with a project that encapsulates the tensions of modern architecture: between icon and infrastructure, ambition and responsibility.

passages.heading: Burj Al Khalifa: How Many Floors and Stories Does It Have?
passages.text: The Burj Khalifa’s highest floor accessible to the public is the 148th-floor observation deck at 555 meters. A second observation deck sits on the 124th floor at 452 meters. Above level 156, the structure transitions from concrete to steel, and the spire adds 242.6 meters to reach a total Burj Khalifa height in feet of 2,722 (829.8 meters to tip)—roughly three times the Eiffel Tower and nearly twice the Empire State Building.

passages.heading: Structural Innovation and Engineering Intelligence
passages.text: The Burj Khalifa illustrates how computational modeling, material science, and collaborative design have become central to architectural practice. The construction required 330,000 cubic meters of concrete, 55,000 tonnes of steel rebar, and 22 million man-hours of labor. For architects and students of high-rise engineering, the building serves as a reminder that visionary architecture must be underpinned by rigorous technical intelligence.

828 metres tall, Burj Khalifa is a mixed-use skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. It ranks first among the world's tallest completed buildings by architectural height. [2]

INSIDE THE ENGINEERING

How Burj Khalifa was built.

Design, structure and construction. Technical sources reviewed 9 September 2026.

SOM arranged three concrete wings around a six-sided core. Each wing braces the other two, while the central cell supplies torsional stiffness. The setback geometry aligns columns above with walls below, avoiding disruptive transfers as the floor plate reduces. Gravity and lateral resistance follow the same disciplined geometry.

A reinforced-concrete mat, 3.7 metres thick, distributes the tower load to bored piles 1.5 metres in diameter and 43 metres long. The mat was cast in four pours totalling 12,500 cubic metres. Low-permeability concrete forms part of the foundation durability strategy.

The Samsung C&T, Six Construct and Arabtec joint venture had to coordinate cranes, labour and material supply vertically. BESIX reports concrete pumping to 585 metres and cycles reaching two floors per week. Special mixes and predominantly night-time pours addressed temperatures exceeding 45°C.

Successive setbacks change the shape the wind encounters, reducing coherent vortex formation. The envelope uses silver-coated glazing to limit solar gain. Mechanical equipment is distributed through double-height service floors; the design also collects air-conditioning condensate for reuse. The steel spire was assembled inside the building and hydraulically raised into position.

passages.heading: Burj Khalifa
passages.text: The **Burj Khalifa**<sup>[a]</sup> (previously known as **Burj Dubai** prior to inauguration) is a megatall skyscraper in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Designed by the SOM architectural firm, it is the world's tallest structure, with a total height of 829.8 m (2,722 ft, or just over half a mile) and a roof height (excluding the antenna, but including a 242.6 m spire)<sup>[2]</sup> of 828 m (2,717 ft). It has been the tallest building in the world since its complete inauguration in 2011, surpassing Taipei 101, which had held the record since 2004.<sup>[3]</sup><sup>[4]</sup>

passages.heading: Burj Khalifa
passages.text: The design is derived from the Islamic architecture of the region, such as the Great Mosque of Samarra. The Y-shaped tripartite floor geometry is designed to optimise residential and hotel space. A buttressed central core and wings support the height of the building. Its central core houses all vertical transportation except egress stairs within each of the wings.<sup>[7]</sup> The structure also features a cladding system which is designed to withstand Dubai's hot summer temperatures.<sup>[8]</sup> The Burj Khalifa has 57 elevators and 8 escalators.
